current_episode.title: The future of energy security: The role of gas networks

guest.bio_context: James Earl runs Future Energy Networks, the membership organisation for the UK's gas networks, representing National Gas and the four gas distribution networks in Great Britain, as well as Northern Irish Gas Networks. His career background spans both gas and electricity sectors, giving him insight into how the two energy vectors interact with each other.

So I guess I start with talking about what are green gases So there are several different green gases I start with biomethane which is the one that we already have in our grid today So biomethane is the same methane effectively as fossil fuel methane that we use today, but it's produced from organic material rather than from fossil fuels, meaning that it's low carbon or even ca

pending_qa.q: How can green gases like biomethane complement renewable electricity in future energy systems?
pending_qa.r: According to James Earl, biomethane is already in the grid today at about 1% of gas use, and could potentially meet between a fifth or a sixth of current demand in the future. Beyond biomethane, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage will be needed as part of the energy system for industry and power generation when renewables are not producing. The future for gas and gas networks will be 'multi-molecule' with lots of different green molecules working in partnership with electrification.

pending_qa.q: Why are data centers increasingly connecting to gas networks instead of waiting for electricity connections?
pending_qa.r: Data centers are looking at the gas network because they are being quoted up to 15 years for electricity infrastructure connections, which simply doesn't work for their operational timelines. Gas networks are currently still connecting more new connections than disconnecting from the network, and data centers represent a growing area of interest.

pending_qa.q: What is the current status of gas network decommissioning in the UK?
pending_qa.r: James Earl emphasizes that the starting point for the conversation about getting rid of gas and decommissioning is not where the industry is at the moment. The reality is that gas networks are still connecting more new connections to the network than they are disconnecting, and the gas network is growing. He argues that rushing to decommission gas infrastructure would cause bills to shoot through the roof and is not the right approach for customers.

pending_qa.q: How should policymakers balance decarbonization, affordability, and energy security in the energy transition?
pending_qa.r: James Earl explains that energy policy should not focus solely on decarbonization but rather on the trilemma of decarbonization, affordability, and security of supply. The conversation should be about how to use existing world-class gas infrastructure in partnership with electrical infrastructure to get the right outcome for customers, rather than rushing to decommission the gas network.

pending_qa.q: What role should gas networks play in managing peak demand in future energy systems?
pending_qa.r: Gas networks do an incredible job today in managing real peaks in demand, and James Earl believes this capability should remain central to future energy system design. The approach should use gas and green gases to keep the system secure and deal with extreme events and peaks, while using electricity and electrification to fill in the gaps around that, rather than using gas everywhere or relying on it as much as today.
